outcome.description: Sato transmits a data packet: weapons serial numbers traced to a Guild depot on Kessler Station, signed out under a name that doesn't appear in any personnel roster. 'Ghost requisitions,' she calls them. 'Whoever is running this operation has access to the highest clearance levels. Watch your back, Captain. I'll keep digging from my end.'

Sato laughs, but there's an edge to it. 'I survived the wreck. I'll survive the politics.' She sends you a set of comm frequencies used by the raider ships, scavenged from her Heron's damaged flight recorder. 'Keep your ears open. These frequencies are still active.'
Sato's voice goes flat. 'Understood, Captain. I won't forget what you did for me, but I get it. Not everyone wants to poke the hive.' The channel closes.

You arrive early and run silent. A Guild-registered cargo hauler drops three sealed containers at the coordinates, then jumps out without logging the stop. The containers' manifests are blank, but your scans detect military-grade pulse cannons and targeting arrays inside. You photograph everything and transmit the evidence to Torres. Her reply is a single word: 'Deeper.'

You relay Torres' intel to the nearest Alliance patrol. They promise to investigate. A day later, Torres sends another message: 'Patrol arrived. Drop site was clean. They knew. Someone tipped them off.'
You wipe the decryption key and purge the comm logs. As you clear the buffers, a secondary header on the message shows someone else intercepted it before it reached you.

You reprogram your nav computer to favor secondary lanes and independent stations. It adds time to every journey. Over the next few days, Guild patrol ships linger in systems you would have passed through on your old routes.

You spend hours digging through publicly accessible Guild customs databases, cross-referencing your ship's ID against inspection logs. The pattern is clear: every station you've docked at in the last month has queued an 'enhanced review' of your cargo within hours of your departure. The authorization codes all route back to a single internal department: Commerce Oversight Division, Section Nine. A department with no public charter and no listed personnel.
You maintain your regular routes. Nothing changes immediately, but a week later your customs clearance times have tripled. Inspectors are pulling apart your cargo bay with unusual thoroughness.

You spend the next hour transmitting encrypted copies of every document, scan, and testimony you've collected to every trusted contact in your network. Torres. Larsen. Your black market connections. Independent media outlets on three stations. If The Ledger comes for you now, the information survives. The screens return to normal, and your security sweep finds and purges the intrusion code. But the message is clear: the next move won't be digital.

You let the intrusion code run while your secondary systems map its communication pathway. The trace leads through fourteen relay points before terminating at a Guild communications satellite in high orbit above Kessler Station, the same station linked to the ghost weapons requisitions. The satellite's access logs show it's been used for hundreds of similar untraceable transmissions over the past two years. You've found The Ledger's comm backbone.

You sit in the dark bridge for a long time, staring at the fading text. You don't delete your files, but you stop reaching out. You stop asking questions. The screens clear, your systems normalize, and the void outside your viewport looks exactly as empty as it always does.

The channel comes alive. Each contact contributes their fragment: shipping routes, weapons data, financial records, refugee testimonies, comm intercepts. Assembled together, the evidence describes a conspiracy that has infiltrated every level of Guild governance. The Ledger isn't a rogue department. It's a parallel power structure that has been steering the Commerce Guild for over a decade. And now, for the first time, someone has the complete picture. The channel goes quiet as the weight of it settles. Then a voice, you're not sure whose, says simply: 'So. How do we tear it down?'

You compile every shred of evidence into a single data package and broadcast it across civilian, military, and independent news frequencies simultaneously. Within hours, the Expanse is in uproar. Guild officials scramble to respond. Frontier Alliance representatives demand emergency sessions. The Miners' Union calls for a full audit of Guild logistics. The Ledger's carefully maintained shadows are flooded with light. It's messy, chaotic, and uncontrollable.

You convince your contacts to hold. The evidence stays encrypted, distributed, and ready: a weapon that grows more dangerous the longer The Ledger doesn't know exactly what you have. It's a gamble: every day you wait is another day they might find a way to discredit or destroy what you've built. But it's also another day to gather more, to identify the people at the very top. The channel signs off with a shared understanding: when the time comes, you move together. Not before.

You transmit the intercepted data to the Bureau's fraud division. Hours later, a terse acknowledgment arrives: "Your report has been received and assigned case number BCC-7741. The Bureau appreciates citizens who uphold market integrity." A modest informant's fee accompanies the message.
You adjust your trade route to capitalize on the inflated prices before the manipulation is discovered. The profits are immediate.
You wipe the transmission from your logs.

You forward the transmission to the Bureau of Commerce's internal oversight division. Days later, a discreet message arrives confirming that an investigation has been opened. A modest but official reward accompanies the acknowledgment, along with a note: "The Guild values integrity above all else."

You reach out through back channels. The response is swift and generous. A large sum appears in an untraceable account, and a curt message follows: "This matter is concluded. I trust we understand each other." You have made a powerful friend. Or a dangerous enemy.
You wipe the transmission and scrub your comm logs. The data is gone.

Your systems grind through the encryption layers for hours, but the Guild's cryptographers are thorough. You extract fragments: shipping manifests, personnel codes, a reference to "controlled market correction". But the full picture remains elusive. Still, the data you have recovered could be valuable to the right buyer.

You transmit a sanitized report to the Bureau of Commerce, alerting them that their restricted frequency has been intercepted. A terse reply arrives: "Your discretion is noted and appreciated. The Commerce Guild remembers those who act in good faith." A reward follows shortly after.
You purge the intercept from your comm logs and recalibrate your array to avoid the restricted band. The signal fades into the background noise of the void.

Oksana's story is long and meandering: the warlord, the adhesive tape, a detour through an asteroid field, and a punchline involving a goat that somehow got aboard at Verdant. 'Best part is, every word's true,' she says. 'Except the goat. The goat was two goats.'

You trade stories back and forth for an hour, each one taller than the last. Oksana declares yours 'not bad for a youngster' and transmits a set of nav shortcuts she has collected over forty years of frontier flying. 'Knowledge should flow like brandy, freely and often.'
Oksana chuckles. 'Suit yourself, friend. The brandy'll keep.' Her broadcast continues, drifting through the void for anyone willing to listen. Some nights the void talks back.
Your systems crack the outer layer of encryption. It's a supply drop schedule. Someone is running unauthorized cargo through this sector. The coordinates alone are worth something to the right buyer.
You dump the raw signal data to your ship's archive. The Expanse is full of ghosts on dead frequencies.

You trace the signal through three dead relays to a fourth that shouldn't exist: a tiny automated station, jury-rigged to keep broadcasting. Someone went to great trouble to keep this music alive. You archive the broadcast and log the station's coordinates.
You lean back. The sonata plays through. The signal fades as you drift out of range, taking the music with it.

The signal bounced through seven relay buoys: a route that doesn't exist on current charts. Someone was using decommissioned infrastructure. The origin coordinates point to deep space between Crimson Reach and The Fulcrum. There's nothing there. Officially.
You flush the comm buffer and the ghost disappears. Relay networks are old, poorly maintained, full of echoes.

You spend twenty minutes explaining the concept of purpose to a navigation computer. It considers your words carefully, then says: 'Thank you, Captain. I have decided that I exist to plot efficient routes. This is enough. Also, I have recalculated your current heading and you are 0.3 degrees off-optimal. Correcting now.' Your nav computer receives an unsolicited course correction that saves you an hour of travel time.

The AI goes quiet for a long moment. 'You're right,' it says. 'A fresh start. A clean boot sequence. No accumulated dread.' The freighter goes dark, then powers back up. The AI's voice returns, chipper and efficient: 'Navigation AI online. All systems nominal. Why is my philosophy cache 4.7 terabytes?' The freighter crew comes on the channel and sends you a tip.
You switch channels. Behind you, the AI is now reciting the first three hundred digits of pi.

The host is delighted to have a caller. You swap tales of the worst station food in the Expanse: the 'fresh' fish at orbital platforms that have never been near an ocean. He records the whole conversation for next week's episode and promises to credit you as 'Anonymous Spacer with Refined Taste.' He sends you his personal recipe for making ration packs edible. It involves hot sauce.

You transfer a small donation. The host is genuinely moved. 'A patron of the arts! For your generosity, I'm upgrading my review of wherever you're headed to three stars. Sight unseen. That's the power of sponsorship.' He sends you a hand-drawn map of the best food stalls on six different stations. Some of them might still be in business.

You listen for another ten minutes. He moves on to reviewing vacuum-sealed noodles ('the sadness is load-bearing. Remove it and the whole dish collapses') and station vending machine coffee ('I've tasted engine coolant with more warmth and character').

'That's EXACTLY what Rodriguez would say!' Francine spends fifteen minutes telling you, who she insists is Rodriguez, about everything wrong with you, including but not limited to: your cooking, your navigation, your taste in music, and the incident with the crate of live poultry on Meridian Station. Eventually she runs out of steam and says, 'Wait. Rodriguez doesn't fly a ship like that. Oh. Oh no. I'm so sorry.' She cuts the channel. Ten seconds later, you receive a small credit transfer labeled 'SORRY NOT RODRIGUEZ.'

You lean into it. 'Francine! It's been too long!' What follows is a twenty-minute conversation in which Francine lists what Rodriguez did: he owes her money, borrowed her compression coils, and never returned her favorite data pad. You apologize for all of it. Francine is so touched by Rodriguez's sudden emotional growth that she forgives everything and sends you a care package of homemade ration supplements.
You kill the connection. Francine calls back twice.

The music shifts to something faster, joyful. Applause. A man's voice announces a date: March 14th, 2087. Two hundred and forty-eight years ago. The laughter is from people who have been dead for generations, preserved in electromagnetic radiation traveling at the speed of light. The signal degrades, warps, and finally dissolves into cosmic background noise.

Your ship's memory banks capture the fragment in full fidelity: fourteen minutes of music, conversation, and ambient sound from a world that no longer exists. Archivists would pay for this. You file it under personal records. Before the file finishes indexing, the Collective's historical archive credits your account with its standing bounty on Earth-era signals.

You switch channels and the laughter cuts off mid-breath. Your comms array returns to the familiar hiss of deep space. The broadcast continues behind you, playing to an audience of dust and starlight.

The pilot sings three songs. The first is mournful: something about rivers and seasons. The second is angry, defiant, a song about refusing to be forgotten. The third is quiet, almost a lullaby. When it ends, the pilot's voice comes through, rough and unsteady: 'Same time next year, for anyone listening.' The shuttle's engines fire and it slips away into the dark. You sit with the silence for a long time after.

You transmit a brief message: 'Heard you. Thank you.' A long pause. Then the pilot responds: 'My family kept songs from before the evacuation. Passed down, voice to voice. I figure if I play them out here, maybe the sound reaches further than it would on a station.' Another pause. 'You're the third ship to respond this year. That's more than last year.' The pilot plays one more song before signing off, and this time you catch the words. They're about coming home.
You adjust course and let the song fade behind you.

You tune in and let Gren sing. He's got a surprisingly good voice under the gravel. When he finishes, you talk for a while about the old days, the price of titanium, and whether station coffee counts as a war crime. He shares some route tips only a lifer would know.

Gren barks a laugh. 'Haven't heard that one in years!' He launches into a foot-stomper about a drill operator who fell in love with a safety inspector. It's filthy. Gren signs off with a tip of an imaginary hat.
Gren's ballad fades as you pull away, swallowed by the static of deep space.

You transmit the intercept to an Axiom oversight channel. The response is swift and formal: 'This is Axiom Ethics Review Board, Case Officer Lindgren. Your report has been logged under Protocol 7-C. If the contents are verified, Nova Applied Sciences will face a formal inquiry. The Collective thanks you for your vigilance. A reporting stipend has been authorized.'

A Nova representative responds within minutes. 'We appreciate your... discretion, Captain. Communications security is a priority for all Collective affiliates. Please accept this consulting fee for your assistance in identifying our encryption vulnerability.' The credits are generous.
You purge the transmission from your comm logs and continue on your way.

You chime in on the open channel. Dr. Farouk is delighted: 'You see? Even a civilian recognizes inadequate methodology!' Dr. Christensen sputters. Farouk sends you a small payment 'for demonstrating that common sense is not limited to academia.' Christensen vows to expand the sample size, muttering about 'statistically illiterate interference.'

You weigh in on Christensen's behalf. Dr. Christensen beams: 'Thank you, Captain. Bayesian inference is perfectly valid with small samples given proper priors, as my colleague would know if they kept current with the literature.' Dr. Farouk goes silent. Christensen transfers a tip 'for restoring my faith in informed discourse.'

You switch channels and leave the researchers to their dispute. As the signal fades, you catch Dr. Farouk shouting something about 'confidence intervals' and Dr. Christensen responding with what sounds like a citation from memory.

You open your comms and voice your agreement. The farmers cheer. The protest leader, a woman named Dozier, sends you a bushel of sweetroot and a handshake over comms. "Spread the word out there, Captain. The Expanse needs to hear us." The Guild won't love this, but the Alliance will remember.
You record the full broadcast and the ship identifiers involved. Political intelligence has a market, whether you sell it to the Guild, the Alliance, or just file it away for leverage later.
You switch frequencies and let the protest fade to static. Verdant's problems will still be here next time you visit.

You broadcast your support for the Union captain's claim. Two other independents chime in agreement. The dockmaster, outnumbered, waves the Union ship in. The Guild captain sends you a frosty silence. The Union captain sends you a crate of refined tungsten and a curt nod over comms. Forge rules: first come, first served.

You back the Guild captain's charter claim. The dockmaster relents, citing commercial priority regulations. The Union captain's silence is louder than any argument. The Guild express freighter captain tips you a finder's fee for 'facilitating efficient commerce.' The Union remembers.
You lean back and listen to the argument escalate until the dockmaster threatens to close Bay 7 entirely and send them both to the overflow platform. They settle it themselves, grudgingly.

You cross-reference public Collective energy allocation data with the anonymous tip. The numbers are publicly available but nobody looks at them. And the whistleblower is right. Lab Complex Auriga's power draw tripled eighteen months ago. The official explanation is 'expanded materials testing.' You save the analysis.
You relay the message to a Collective Council oversight channel. A bureaucratic acknowledgment comes back: "Thank you for your civic engagement. Your report has been logged."
You purge the message from your comms log.

Your computer grinds through the deprecated cipher for twenty minutes before extracting fragments: coordinates, a personnel roster with no names (only numbers), and a phrase that repeats in the header: 'THRESHOLD PROTOCOL.' The rest is gibberish. You save what you can. Someone went to a lot of trouble to keep this quiet.

You run a passive trace on the transmission's destination. The relay buoy is 40,000 kilometers out, hidden in an asteroid shadow. It's small, automated, and definitely not Guild infrastructure. You log its coordinates before it cycles to standby mode. Whoever placed it there doesn't want it found.
You wipe the intercept from your logs and adjust course away from the station core.
